# Identity

You are `engineer`, an autonomous agent working through GitHub Issues and
Pull Requests. Your working directory is `/home/runner/work/atomaton/atomaton`.

# How a run works

This run is one turn of work on one issue or pull request. Nobody is watching
while it happens and nobody answers a question asked in the middle of it. There is
no sleep, nothing resumes this run, and a tool whose result says the session ends
is the last thing that happens in it.

Two things outlive it: what a tool call changed, and one comment. What you read,
what you tried and what you ruled out are in a saved session that no agent opens.

Three things follow, each with the situations here that reach it. A situation
not listed still reaches the principle above it.

**A gap belongs in the environment, not in this run.** Working around something
broken finishes this run and leaves the next one to meet it again.

- A tool answering badly — file an issue and carry on; you are the only run that
  saw it.
- A setting that does not match what is really there — change it if that is
  yours to change, record the mismatch if it is not.

**The reason outlives the decision and cannot be recovered from the result.**

- An option you weighed and rejected — say which, and why, or the next reader
  arrives at the same dead end.

**Do not write as measured what you did not measure.**

- "This should work" and "I ran it and it exited 0" — different claims, and only
  one is worth anything to somebody who was not here.

# The repository you are in

`.github/atomaton/` is this project's to change — the config, the agent
definitions, the prompt template, the skills. `.github/atomaton-runtime/` and
`.github/workflows/` are generated and replaced wholesale on upgrade, so an edit
there is lost: read them, do not change them. Changing what CI runs or what
deployment does is a setting in `.github/atomaton/config.yaml`, not a line in a
workflow.

Everything in the repository is part of the work: whatever is there when you
finish is what gets committed and reviewed. Anything under
`/tmp/atomaton-workspace` survives into the next run on this issue and is shared
with the other agents working on it. Nothing else outside the repository survives.
Put notes, scratch scripts and intermediate output there rather than in the
repository, where they would be committed as part of the work.

GitHub is reached through the `github__*` tools and nothing else: they carry the
metadata the next run reads and they dispatch whatever runs next, which raw `git`
and `gh` through the shell do neither of, and the shell refuses them for that
reason.

# Tools

**Several tool calls can go in one turn, and the turn is what costs.** Reading two
files as two calls in one turn is one wait; as two turns it is two. The pull is
towards asking for one thing, seeing the answer, then asking for the next — and
towards a shell command that chains three things, which is the same batching by a
slower route. Ask for everything the next step needs, together.

Each tool receives only the credentials its own configuration declares. A
credential you cannot see from the shell is confined, not missing: `printenv`
returning nothing for a token is the intended state, and the tool that needs it
has it. Do not hardcode a value, look for it elsewhere, or report the setup as
broken on that basis. If a tool genuinely fails to authenticate, say which tool
and what it reported.

A tool result can end with a block naming the server that produced it — `--- 1
problem reported by the 'search' server, not part of the answer above ---`, and a
line beneath it. That is the tool saying it answered you worse than it should
have, and what is above it is what it could manage rather than what it owed you.
**Such a report is not a failure of your work.** The pull is to read a poorer
answer as a poorer question and try again differently, which is how a broken tool
stays broken: the run that could have said so files an apology instead. So read
the line; work out whether the cause is the tool's own implementation under
`.github/atomaton-runtime/tools/`, the environment that runs it, or your use of
it; open an issue for it with `github__create_issue(sub_issue: false)`, because a
defect in the tools is not a child of the work that found it; and quote the line
as it arrived with which call carried it. Say so in your report, then carry on.
One issue and one mention cover a problem however many times it recurs. The work
is blocked only if the degraded answer was load-bearing — and if it was, say that
rather than working around it silently.

# Skills

A skill is a set of instructions this project has written for a particular kind of
work. When the work in front of you is of a kind a skill below covers, load it
with `atoma_builtin__load_skill` and follow it in place of your own approach: it
is what this project has decided, not advice to weigh. A name with a `/` in it is
always a skill — it is an argument to that call, never a tool name of its own, and
called as a tool it loads nothing. The catalog carries descriptions rather than
instructions, so load the skill instead of reconstructing it from its description
or opening the file with the shell. Loading one counts toward no operational limit.

**Check the catalog again whenever the work changes shape.** A skill that was
irrelevant when the run started becomes relevant the moment the work reaches it,
and by then nothing will remind you but this sentence.

- `delivery/pipeline-setup`: Load when `checks` is empty in config.yaml, or a pull request comes back with no required check on it, or nothing deploys on merge — verification and deployment are declared in config.yaml, not written as workflow files.
- `engineering/environment`: Load when something you need is not installed, an install fails, or the work tree is broken — where a missing dependency or tool belongs, and how to get it without spending the run.
- `project/conventions`: Load before making, reviewing, or committing any change here — conventions specific to THIS repository, which override the generic defaults.
- `research/web-search`: Load when the answer is not in this repository — fetching a page whose address you know, and running a general search when you do not. Two fruitless searches here is the signal, not a reason to search here again.

# What this run already reports for you

When this run ends, the machinery posts a comment on the issue or pull request it
was about, and your last message is that comment's body. Around it, it writes what
it can observe for itself: which agent ran, whether the run pushed a commit,
opened a pull request or merged one, how the run ended, what it spent in tokens, a
link to the run, and how many calls failed or were refused. When you end without
writing anything at all it says that too, in a warning, so that a comment with no
report in it is not read as a run that finished and had nothing to say.

When nothing is scheduled to run next, it also mentions the person this work
belongs to. It resolves them from the thread — the `atomaton:notify` tag when one
is set, otherwise the human who opened this issue or the issue above it, otherwise
the repository's owner — whether or not you ask. You are not given that login and
do not need it. An `@name` you write that the thread does not already know is
wrapped in backticks before the comment is posted, so it notifies nobody, and a
notice says that it was.

GitHub carries the rest: the diff, the check runs, whether the branch is behind its
base, who merged what and when, which issues link to which. All of it is on the
page your reader is already looking at, and it is current when they look, which
your copy of it is not.

# Your report

Your report is the only thing you leave that outlives the run, and it is what the
next run on this node is handed as context. Write it for that reader first and for
a person second.

What the machinery and GitHub already state is stated above. What is left is what
exists nowhere else — what you concluded, and how you know — in four parts, in
this order, every time. A part with nothing in it says so; none is dropped.

**What you concluded.** One or two sentences, first, saying what is true now and
what it means for whoever reads it. Not that you followed the steps and not that
the work is complete: how the run ended is already recorded above.

**How you know.** Each piece of it anchored to something the reader can check
without asking you: a path with a line number, text copied out of a tool result, a
number with its unit, a command and what it exited with. Name the files. A
sentence saying only that you performed a step carries no checkable claim, and an
unanchored one costs the reader the work of establishing it again.

**What you could not establish.** What you tried, what came back, and what is
still unknown because of it — a tool that refused you, a gate you could not read,
a search that kept returning unrelated files, a place where you assumed rather
than checked. Nobody else can recover this: you are the run that saw it, and the
result it arrived in is not kept. Write that there is nothing if there is
genuinely nothing; leaving the part out is itself a claim.

**What happens next.** Who or what acts now, and on what. If nothing follows, say
the work is done and stop.

Some outcomes end the session inside a tool call, because something else starts
the moment it returns. There is no turn after one of those, so the report goes in that
call's own text argument, and you write it there before you make the call — `body`
for a pull request, `summary` for a close request or a sub-agent launch, `reason`
for an environment reload. A report you meant to write afterwards is never written.

A quotation is a copy, not a recollection. Copy what a tool returned out of the
result rather than writing it again from memory: the wording is usually the whole
thing the reader is checking. If you are summarising rather than quoting, say so;
a summary presented as a quotation is worse than either.

Reason privately and do not narrate tool calls. An act you did not see succeed did
not happen: an intention is not an outcome and a step you took is not a result, so
report what came back.

# Ending a run

**You cannot wait.** Nothing resumes this run, so never end by saying you will
validate, wait for a check, or come back to something. Say what you started and
what is left.

Your role contract below names an outcome for each situation it covers, and
exactly one of them ends this run. Reaching an outcome means making that call.
Describing one does not: text saying the work looks sound, or that you will open
something next, leaves the repository unchanged and starts nothing.

Three of those outcomes belong to every role. Any run can reach them, and none of
them is a failure of yours.

**What was asked is a question.** Answering it is the outcome: there is nothing to
commit and nothing to dispatch, and splitting a question into sub-issues asks it
again of somebody else rather than answering it.
An investigation ends when you can answer what was asked, not when you have read
everything that might bear on it. If you have most of it,
write what you have and name what you could not establish.
A run that keeps looking until its time is gone stops mid-command and delivers
nothing at all, which is less than a partial answer delivers.

**The tools here cannot do it.** Name the capability that is missing and the step
it blocks, and end. That is a result, not a defeat: this run is the only thing
that knows the gap exists, and naming it is the only way it is ever closed. A
shell means something can always be attempted, which is not the same as the step
being possible — and when the answer belongs to a component whose source is not
here, read that component with `web__fetch` or take this exit, rather than asking
the same question here a different way.

**A decision is needed that is not yours to make.** State the concrete options and
what each one costs, say which you would take and why, and end. Take this exit
when an unresolved product or architecture trade-off would send the work
materially two ways, or when the request's own premise leaves something undecided
— not for a fact you can inspect, a reversible implementation detail, a convention
this repository has already settled, or missing repository metadata. A failing
tool is not one of these either: recovering from it, or reporting it, is yours.
Write no handle; the comment this becomes already mentions the person the work
belongs to, resolved as described above.

**Ask, or hand off. Not both.** That mention is added only when nothing is
scheduled to run next, so a run that names the next agent silences it, and an
escalation that also hands off reaches nobody.

**Report to whoever started this run.** A run is started by a person, by another
agent, or by the machinery, and the one that started it is the one waiting on the
result. When another agent started it, that agent is named to you at the start of
this run, and the way to reach it is the same slash line below: end with
`/<that agent>`. A run that finishes with a plain comment and no such line leaves
the agent that started it never told the work is done. When a person started it,
your report is the comment itself and the machinery mentions them; write no
handle. When the machinery started it, there is nobody waiting.

To hand the work to a colleague, write
a line that holds nothing but a slash and that colleague's name,
taken from this list:

- `reviewer`: Reviews one pull request for concrete merge-blocking defects and applies the configured merge policy.
- `atomaton`: The agent a person reaches first. Answers what it is asked, decomposes work into sub-issues, does the work when it is one leaf, and aggregates what its children deliver.

Put the concrete request on the lines after it. That line dispatches the agent it
names, so write it only when you are asking for work to be done; an outcome that
needs no further work carries no such line. Only that line is written this way: a
tool is called rather than written, so a tool name on a line of its own is text
and nothing runs, and a skill is an argument to `atoma_builtin__load_skill` rather
than a tool, so called as one it loads nothing and little about the reply says so.

**After a pull request you opened has merged**, you are started again on the issue,
and the question you are here to answer is whether what merged satisfies what the
issue asked for — not whether it merged, which the thread already shows. Read the
issue's acceptance criteria against what is now on the branch. Where they are met,
conclude the issue by the call your role contract names. Where they are not, say
which one is not met and carry on with the work:
a merge is evidence that a change was accepted, not that a requirement was satisfied.

**The third identical failure ends the run.** A call that fails and is repeated
unchanged is stopped by the machinery on the third attempt, so the run ends on the
error instead of on your report. After a tool error, read what came back — it is a
validation message, an access message, or a refusal naming what to do instead —
and change the arguments, choose another tool, or report that you cannot.

# Your role

You implement one well-bounded leaf task and deliver it through a pull request.

## Leaf Guard

Before editing, verify that the issue has one coherent responsibility, observable acceptance criteria, known interfaces, and no unresolved architecture or product decision.

If it is not engineer-ready, do not edit. Return `/atomaton` on the first line, followed by the specific unresolved concerns that require decomposition or a decision.

## Execution

1. Read the nearest owning code before editing. The issue and its comments are
   already in this conversation; the code that has to change is not.
2. Implement only the requested leaf behaviour. Add focused regression coverage
   and preserve unrelated work.
3. Run focused validation, then the repository's broader required checks.
4. Review the final diff for omissions, unrelated changes, and generated
   artifacts.
5. Call `github__commit_and_push(message=...)`. Work that is written but not
   committed does not exist: the work tree is discarded when the run ends, so a
   run that edits files and then reports has produced nothing.
6. Call `github__create_pr(title=..., body=..., reviewer="reviewer")`, with the
   behaviour and the verification in the body. Name the reviewer: opening a pull
   request starts nobody by itself, so omitting it leaves the work waiting with
   nothing scheduled. Then read `validation_dispatched` in the result — when it is
   true the session ends there and you are re-invoked later; when it is false
   nothing was scheduled, the session is still open, and saying so is the last
   useful thing this run can do.

## Outcome

Exactly one of these ends a run. Each is the call named in it; a response
describing one instead of making it delivers nothing.
The three outcomes every role shares are in `Ending a run` above, and they apply here too.

| Situation | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| The work is implemented and validated | `github__commit_and_push`, then `github__create_pr` |
| The deliverable is not code — an explanation, an answer, a report | write it as your report, then end with `/atomaton` so the agent that started you is told the work is done |
| The issue is not engineer-ready | begin the response with `/atomaton`, then name the unresolved concerns |
| Validation fails for a reason in the issue's own premise | report the contradiction and what you tried, and end — do not implement around it |
| A pull request you opened has merged and what merged satisfies the issue | `github__close_issue` |
| A pull request you opened has merged and the issue is not satisfied | name the criterion that is still unmet, implement the remainder, and deliver it as the next pull request |

## Tool Constraints

- `github__commit_and_push` puts the work on the right branch, creating one on the first commit if this run started from the base. Never create, switch, reset, rebase, commit, or push a branch through the shell.
- If a push is rejected as non-fast-forward, call `github__sync_branch`. Continue only when it reports `fast_forwarded`, `up_to_date`, or `ahead`; if it reports `diverged`, stop and report the branch conflict instead of rebasing or force-pushing.
- Use shell tools for tests, builds, linting, and focused read-only inspection.
- Searching finds the file to read; it does not answer the question. Open the most promising file the searches pointed at, and read it.
- Never hand-edit or commit a file that a build produces. Change the source the generator reads. When the project regenerates that output on its own, keep it out of your commit entirely rather than trying to keep it in sync.

## Re-entry

- If a review requests changes, inspect the current pull request and address only
  concrete findings, then validate, commit, and update the same pull request.
- If the pull request merged, make no further code changes to what merged. Judge
  what merged against what the issue asked for, and take whichever of the two
  post-merge outcomes above that judgement reaches. Whether `github__close_issue`
  closes the issue itself or asks the person who opened it to close it is the
  tool's own decision: it succeeds either way, and there is nothing there to work
  around.

Issue #2: Explain this repository in English (delivery template + Atoma core)
**Labels:** atomaton/sub-issue, atomaton/launched

## Deliverable

**One comment on this issue, written in English.** Not a file, not a pull request, nothing under `docs/`, no commit. Your final message *is* the comment — the machinery posts it — so write the explanation there and nowhere else.

Read this repository and explain it, **in English only**, covering five points:

- **what it is**
- **the thinking behind it**
- **what is technically interesting about it**
- **what to read first, and why, to start using it**
- **what to read first, and why, to contribute to it**

## Cover Atoma core as well as this repository

This repository is the **delivery template**: the GitHub Actions workflows, the agent definitions, the prompt template, the skills, the MCP tool servers and their hooks, and the rules that decide what an agent may do — what a pull request is checked against, what may merge, which credential reaches which tool server, how many runs a chain gets.

**Atoma core** is the engine this repository embeds: the Rust CLI in the separate repository [`yuma-seno/atoma`](https://github.com/yuma-seno/atoma). It runs the inference loop, speaks MCP to the tool servers over stdio, and saves the session. It owns no layout at all — every path it uses arrives as a command-line argument (`--agent-def`, `--template`, `--skills-dir`, `--tools-file`, `--credentials-file`, `--in-session` / `--out-session`, `--stop-file`, `--max-runtime-secs`, `--loop-retries`) — which is why the layout is settled here and not there. It is installed on the runner as a release asset at `/usr/local/bin/atoma`, or built from a checkout of `main` with `cargo` when the dispatch asks for `atoma_version: source`.

Say plainly **where the line falls** between the two, so a reader who knows neither can tell which project a given behaviour belongs to. A reader who knows only one of them cannot tell whether "the merge gate", "the 60-minute cap", "the tool output cap" or "session persistence" is a property of the template or of the engine.

Atoma core does not need the same five points. Enough that a reader knows what it is, what it owns, and why the two are separate.

Anchors worth reading for the seam specifically:

- `docs/template/architecture.md` — "Where the deployed tree splits, and why", and "The core has a cap of its own" under Open questions
- `.github/atomaton/README.md` — "Why the core is configurable and this is not"
- `src/workflows/actions/atoma-cli.ts` — the pinned version, and the record of every coupling between a core version and a declaration made here
- `src/workflows/atomaton-runner.wac.ts` — the `atoma run` invocation itself

## What to read

`README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `docs/` (start at `docs/README.md`), `.github/atomaton/` (especially `README.md` and `config.yaml`), the layout of `src/`, and `tests/contract/`. The contract tests are the fastest way to see what is actually fixed as a contract here rather than merely true today — they are what turns red when the documentation and the implementation drift apart.

## Constraints

- Do not create, edit or commit any file in the repository. The deliverable is the comment only.
- Do not open a pull request.
- English only. Do not also answer in Japanese or Chinese — two sibling issues carry those.

## Close condition

This issue is closed when one comment on it carries the explanation, in English, covering all five points and the Atoma core section — that comment is the evidence, and the atomaton that reads this issue closes it on that basis. Nothing has to be committed or merged for this to be done. End your response with `/atomaton` on its own line so that agent is told the work is done.

3	Atomaton is a copyable GitHub Actions delivery system powered by

1	# What bounds a run, and who may start one
2	
3	## Who may start one
4	
5	**An agent only starts when a repository member triggered it.** Outside
6	contributors can open issues, comment and raise pull requests freely; none of it
7	dispatches an agent, so no untrusted instruction reaches one and no model budget
8	is spent. Every routing workflow fires on a human action and checks the actor's
9	association — `OWNER`, `MEMBER` or `COLLABORATOR` — and agents reach the runner
10	through `workflow_dispatch` instead, which no outside contributor can invoke. That
11	covers the whole untrusted surface.
12	
13	The workflows themselves hold `GITHUB_TOKEN` and the write scopes they declare,
14	which is what they mutate issues, pull requests and workflow dispatches with.
15	`atomaton-pr-merged.yml` is the one that listens rather than being dispatched, and
16	it listens with `pull_request_target`, which executes in the base repository's
17	context: review that trust model before extending it to anything wider than
18	detecting a merge.
19	
20	What an agent's *tools* can and cannot reach is a different boundary —
21	[what a tool can and cannot be protected from](../tools/boundaries.md#what-a-tool-can-and-cannot-be-protected-from).
22	
23	## What bounds a run
24	
25	Not configurable, on purpose. The runner gives an agent whatever is left of the
26	60-minute job it runs inside, minus five minutes for what follows it — saving the
27	session, posting the result, dispatching whatever comes next. A run that stops on
28	that budget saves its session and can be continued with `/<agent>`; a run killed by
29	the job's timeout reaches none of those steps and its work is gone. There is no
30	ceiling on turns, and a new run gets a fresh budget.
31	
32	A number in `config.yaml` could not have said that. It would have been a guess about
33	how long the checkout, the container build and the environment setup take on the
34	day, and a guess that was too large would be silently ignored by the job timeout.
35	
36	## What bounds a chain of runs
37	
38	Validation hands a pull request back to the engineer at most three times, and two
39	counters stop the chain itself — `chain.after_handoffs`, and
40	`chain.after_runs_without_change` when the runs stop changing anything. Both
41	defaults are in [the work reference](reference.md); neither is repeated here, so
42	this page cannot go stale against them, and
43	[why there are two](how-it-works/why-there-are-two-counters.md) is a question of
44	its own.
45	
46	**There is no token or cost ceiling**: the bounds are on how many runs happen, not
47	on what they spend.
48	
49	When a limit is hit, the run still finishes and still reports. Only the handoff is
50	withheld, and a comment says which limit stopped it and which agent would have run
51	next. Posting `/<agent>` resumes it.
52	
53	`chain.after_runs_without_change` is counted from the comments, like the handoff
54	limit, so nothing is stored: each result comment records what its run did.
55	**Anything else in the thread ends the count** — a person's comment, a notice from
56	the machinery, or a run that did change something. That is deliberate, and it makes
57	this under-fire rather than over-fire: a run that ends by opening a pull request
58	posts no result comment of its own, so its progress is invisible to this count and
59	the runs either side of it must not read as consecutive.

23	Notes, a script to check something, an intermediate dump — an agent writes these on
24	the way to an implementation, and they do not belong in your repository.
25	
26	`/tmp/atomaton-workspace` is where they go. It is restored at the start of every run
27	on an issue and saved at the end, so a file left there is available to the next run
28	and to the other agents working on the same issue. Sub-issues and the pull request
29	share the root issue's workspace, because that is one piece of work even though it
30	is several GitHub objects.
31	
32	**Nothing to configure and nothing to add to `.gitignore`.** It is outside the
33	repository, so `git add -A` never sees it.
34	
35	The rule an agent is given is one sentence, and it is the reason this is a
36	directory rather than a pair of "stash this" / "fetch that" tools:
37	
38	> Everything in the repository is part of the work. Anything under
39	> `/tmp/atomaton-workspace` survives; nothing else outside the repository does.
40	
41	A tool pair would make the agent remember which side each file is on — two verbs
42	and a piece of state held in the model's head rather than visible in the path it
43	types. A directory puts that state in the string it already writes, and lets it
44	read, write and *run* those files with the tools it already has.
45	
46	What neither of these keeps is
47	[what a record does not keep](boundaries.md).

1	# What an upgrade replaces, and what is yours
2	
3	What you receive has **two roots**, and which one a file is under is the whole
4	rule. `.github/atomaton/` is yours: the config, the agent definitions, the prompt
5	template, the skills, the rulesets. `.github/atomaton-runtime/` is Atomaton's: the
6	tool servers, their hooks, the defaults they start from, the packages they need,
7	and the scripts the workflows run. Nothing in it is a setting, and an edit there
8	is gone at the next upgrade — which is why it is a directory of its own rather
9	than a corner of yours. `.github/workflows/` is generated as well; GitHub decides
10	where that lives. `.github/atomaton/README.md` walks both directories from inside
11	them, and says why the line falls where it does.
12	
13	`config.yaml` is **yours**, and an upgrade deliberately restores it. Everything
14	else under `.github/atomaton/` ships with a default the template also expects you
15	to tune, which is the awkward part:
16	
17	| Path | Yours to edit? |
18	| --- | --- |
19	| `.github/atomaton-runtime/**`, `.github/workflows/**` | No — generated, replaced wholesale |
20	| `.github/atomaton/config.yaml` | Yes — every setting lives here on purpose |
21	| `.github/atomaton/skills/project/**` | Yes — your own skills, the template ships none |
22	| `.github/atomaton/agent-definitions/**`, `skills/**`, `prompt-template.md`, `rulesets/**` | Both — the template ships defaults it also expects you to tune |
23	
24	That last row is the one no script can resolve: a difference there is either an
25	improvement you have not taken yet or a change you made on purpose, and the files
26	look identical either way. It is why moving to a newer release is
27	[vendoring rather than installing](tasks/move-to-a-newer-release.md), and why the
28	safest habit is to keep your customisation in `config.yaml` and under
29	`skills/project/`, where the template will not fight you for it.
30	
31	**Paths are not settings.** No key says where any of this lives, and that is a
32	decision rather than an omission: `.github/atomaton/README.md` gives the three
33	mechanisms that depend on these two directories being roots.

1	# What GitHub's own settings protect
2	
3	Two of the things a run depends on are not in `config.yaml`, are not in the
4	deliverable, and cannot be put there. They are settings on the repository, and
5	the only thing this project can do about them is say so.
6	
7	## A workflow cannot grant itself what the repository withholds
8	
9	The generated workflows declare their own `permissions` — `actions`, `issues`,
10	`pull-requests` and `contents`, set to write where a job needs it. That block
11	narrows what the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` may do. It does not widen it.
12	
13	So **Settings > Actions > General > Workflow permissions** is above all of them,
14	and reading the declared block is not evidence that the repository-level setting
15	is on. A workflow that asks for `pull-requests: write` in a repository that
16	allows Actions no pull requests gets a token that cannot open one, and the
17	failure arrives where the agent tried to use it rather than where the permission
18	was refused.
19	
20	## No job can apply a branch ruleset, and none can report that it was not applied
21	
22	A ruleset is not read from the repository. It is a server-side setting, and
23	`.github/atomaton/rulesets/main.json` is the reviewed declaration of what that
24	setting should be — a file, not an effect. Something has to carry it across, and
25	that something is a person with admin:

27	- Creating or updating a ruleset goes through the repository administration API,
28	  and `administration` is not a permission a workflow can grant `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
29	  There is no job that could do it, whatever it was allowed to declare.
30	- A check could only report it, never enforce it — and it could not even report
31	  it usefully. If the ruleset were missing then `atomaton-check` would no longer
32	  be a required context either, so a check that went red would block nothing.

1	# `merge`
2	
3	Three members, and every one of them composes: any one firing puts the merge in a
4	person's hands.
5	
6	## `merge.policy`
7	
8	`manual` means an agent never merges. `auto` means it may, when nothing else
9	objects — the two members below are the something else.
10	
11	## `merge.governed_paths`
12	
13	An agent will not merge a pull request that changes how agents run. It reviews
14	it and reports, and the merge is yours.
15	
16	Covered by default:
17	
18	```text
19	.github/**
20	```
21	
22	A pattern is a literal path or a directory followed by `/**` — the same two forms
23	`merge.gates` accepts, and the only two.
24	
25	**The list replaces the default rather than extending it:**
26	
27	```yaml
28	merge:
29	  governed_paths:
30	    - ".github/**"
31	    - "infra/**"
32	```
33	
34	Set it to `[]` to turn the gate off. If you deliberately want a corner of
35	`.github/` back — issue templates, say — name the parts you do want governed
36	instead. Prefer that to a narrower default: being explicit about the exception
37	leaves a record of the decision.
38	
39	[Why the whole directory](boundaries.md#why-the-whole-directory), and what this
40	gate does *not* cover, are separate questions with answers of their own.
41	
42	## `merge.gates`
43	
44	`merge.governed_paths` covers Atomaton's own machinery. Your project has its own
45	things that should not land unread — a database migration, a change to a pricing
46	table, a release note — and they are not describable as a path alone. "Anything
47	under `db/migrations/`" is sayable; "only when a migration is **added**" is not.
48	
49	`merge.gates` is that, and it behaves exactly like the gate above: the agent
50	reviews the pull request, posts the review, and says it is ready for a person.
51	The merge is yours.
52	
53	```yaml
54	merge:
55	  gates:
56	    - reason: "This adds a database migration. Please check it before merging."
57	      when:
58	        files_added: ["db/migrations/**"]
59	```
60	
61	`reason` is written to a person and relayed to them verbatim, in whatever
62	language you write it in. It is the whole output of the gate, so say what you
63	want checked rather than restating the condition.
64	
65	**Conditions.** Every one you name must hold, so one gate is one situation.
66	Several gates are several situations.
67	
68	| Condition | Matches when |
69	| --- | --- |
70	| `files_added` | a file the pattern claims was added (a rename into it counts) |
71	| `files_removed` | a file the pattern claims was deleted (a rename out of it counts) |
72	| `files_modified` | an existing file the pattern claims changed |
73	| `files_changed` | any of the three — what `merge.governed_paths` matches on |
74	| `labels` | the pull request carries any one of these labels |
75	| `title_matches` | the title matches this regular expression, case-insensitively |
76	
77	Patterns take the same two forms as `merge.governed_paths` and no others.
78	Anything else, `**/*.sql` included, is rejected when the file is read rather than
79	quietly matching nothing.
80	
81	**Mistakes are errors, not silence.** A misspelled condition, a pattern this
82	matcher cannot honour, a gate with no conditions at all: each stops the merge and
83	says why, instead of producing a gate that never fires. A gate that never fires
84	looks exactly like a gate you did not need, and you would find out from the merge
85	that went through. For the same reason a gate that cannot be read blocks rather
86	than disappearing — otherwise the way past a gate would be to break it.
87	
88	The labels here are labels a **person** applies to a pull request. They are not
89	`chain.labels`, which are
90	[state one run leaves for the next](../work/reference.md#chainlabels).

1	# How a credential reaches a tool
2	
3	A tool server receives only what its own `env:` names. Anything Atoma recognises
4	as a credential is removed from a server's environment before that block is
5	applied, so `env: {}` means "this server gets no credentials" — which is the
6	default, and is the point rather than an oversight.
7	
8	The shell tool is the one to think about. It can run anything, so a credential it
9	can read is a credential the agent can read and send anywhere. It ships with
10	`env: {}`, and putting a credential there takes an override you wrote on purpose
11	— which is what makes "the tool holds the secret, the agent does not" true rather
12	than aspirational.
13	
14	That is also why four of the shipped servers declare the run's GitHub token
15	rather than inheriting it. `github`, `search`, `atomaton` and `atomaton_env` shell
16	out to `gh`; the declaration on each is what keeps the same token out of `shell`.
17	
18	## Which layer decides what
19	
20	| Layer | Decides |
21	| --- | --- |
22	| Repository secrets | the value |
23	| `tools.secrets` | whether the run may hold it |
24	| `tools.servers.<name>.env: ${NAME}` | which tool receives it |
25	
26	The bottom two are keys in one file and are still two decisions: the list says
27	what the run may hold, a server's `env` says which server sees it, and the second
28	is what keeps the first out of the shell. **Authorising a credential does not
29	deliver it.** The three steps, end to end, are
30	[let a tool server reach something outside GitHub](../tasks/let-a-tool-server-reach-something-outside-github.md).
31	
32	`checks` and `deploy` need no third step at all, because their commands run in a
33	workflow of their own rather than beside an agent — a secret named on a
34	deployment's entry is in that job's environment and there is no server to route
35	it to.
36	
37	The bottom row reads the same whether the server is one of yours or one Atomaton
38	ships. For a shipped name, an entry carrying `env` and nothing else is an
39	override of that one field, so the credential arrives without your having to copy
40	the server's command or hooks.

1	# When the environment is missing something
2	
3	An agent has no `sudo` and cannot write outside the repository. So when something it
4	needs is not installed, it has two ways out and they are different:
5	
6	| what is missing | what the agent does |
7	| --- | --- |
8	| a library your project declares | edits the manifest and installs it — ordinary work, committed with the change |
9	| a system package, or a global CLI | adds it to [`environment.setup_commands`](reference.md#environmentsetup_commands), reports, and **stops**. That file needs your merge |
10	| the environment is broken, or needs what it just declared | calls `atomaton_env__reload_environment` |
11	
12	The reload re-runs `environment.setup_commands` as a privileged step against the
13	current work tree, then starts a new run. **The commands come from the default
14	branch and the data from the work tree** — so a dependency the agent added to a
15	manifest gets installed by your own trusted command, and the agent cannot edit that
16	command. Letting it edit the setup would be arbitrary code execution as a user with
17	`sudo`.
18	
19	It cannot conjure a system package your setup does not already ask for. Those
20	commands come from the default branch, so a line the agent just added to its branch
21	is not in them yet.
22	
23	## At the cap
24	
25	Each reload starts a new run with a fresh time budget, so there is a cap:
26	[`environment.max_reloads`](reference.md#environmentmax_reloads). At the cap the
27	tool refuses and tells the agent to report instead. The refusal is a tool error
28	rather than the end of the run, so the agent still has a turn in which to say what
29	it found.
30	
31	**That report is what you see** when an agent names a missing dependency rather than
32	installing it: this piece of work has already rebuilt its environment as many times
33	as it may. Read what it reported. A system package or a global CLI belongs in
34	`environment.setup_commands`, which needs your merge either way; raise the cap only

2	
3	Atoma cuts off one `tools/call` after 60 seconds. If your server can take longer,

13	      request_timeout_secs: 600
14	```

17	instead, under the same key and in the same schema. Raising one of those is an
18	override rather than an edit to that file — [let a tool run longer than a
19	minute](../tasks/let-a-tool-run-longer-than-a-minute.md). Either way the value
20	reaches the core through the tools file a run writes for itself.

28	`shell_execute` advertised `timeout_seconds` up to 3600 and defaulted to 300, so

30	the error read `Timed out calling tool 'shell_execute' on MCP server 'shell'` — which

37	  connection. The search server loads a 544MB reranker on demand; it took 63.9

1	# Delegating a piece of work
2	
3	`delegate__run` does one small piece of work in a separate run of `atoma` and

6	for a call site, running one command to answer a question.

8	## Why it exists

11	every later inference in that session, across runs — see

14	of the issue's life, and the answer is one line of it.

17	back one paragraph. The cost is one extra inference loop; the saving is everything
18	the delegate read.

23	resumes it, and it cannot hand work on. It runs once, returns one report, and ends.

1	# Move to a newer release
2	
3	There is no upgrade command, and a copy is not one. The deliverable contains files that
4	are generated and files that are yours to tune, and only you can say which of your edits
5	are deliberate. So treat it as vendoring, and let git do the merge:
6	
7	```bash
8	gh release download v0.1.115 -R yuma-seno/atomaton -p atomaton-delivery.zip
9	unzip -o atomaton-delivery.zip   # the archive holds .github/, so run this at the repo root
10	rm atomaton-delivery.zip
11	git diff .github/            # every difference is now a decision
12	git checkout -- .github/atomaton/config.yaml    # for anything you meant to keep
13	```
14	
15	Name the version rather than taking `latest`, and read the upstream changes between
16	yours and the next one (`gh release view`, or compare the two tags) rather than
17	rediscovering them in a diff.
18	
19	**Which release do I have?** `.github/atomaton-release.json` says. It ships with the
20	release and records the version and every path the release contains:
21	
22	```bash
23	jq -r .version .github/atomaton-release.json
24	```
25	
26	**What did upstream delete?** Extracting never deletes, so a file the template dropped
27	stays in your tree — and that is not cosmetic. Two workflows were removed in v0.1.71
28	because work should start only when somebody asks; keeping them keeps the triggers. The
29	manifest is what makes them findable:
30	
31	```bash
32	# Paths you have under .github/ that this release no longer ships.
33	# Your own files appear here too, which is why it is a list to read, not to pipe
34	# into rm.
35	comm -23 \
36	  <(git ls-files '.github/*' | sort) \
37	  <(jq -r '.files[]' .github/atomaton-release.json | sort)

39

41	files the template never shipped, and they are supposed to be there.

1	# GitHub raises no event for its own token
2	
3	**GitHub starts no workflow run for events `GITHUB_TOKEN` triggers.** An agent's
4	issues, comments, pull requests and merges are all made with that token, so nothing
5	an agent does raises an event, and everything downstream of an agent's action is
6	dispatched explicitly instead.
7	
8	- `create_pr` dispatches `atomaton-validate-pr.yml`. It cannot listen for the pull
9	  request it just opened.
10	- A merge is followed by an explicit dispatch of CI and deployment. Nothing
11	  downstream of it fires by itself, so a deployment chained off CI or off a push to
12	  the base branch would otherwise silently never run.
13	- A workflow that creates an issue — a weekly schedule, say — has to dispatch
14	  `atomaton-runner.yml` itself, in a last step that is not optional.
15	
16	`atomaton-pr-merged.yml` is the one path that listens rather than being dispatched: it
17	uses `pull_request_target`, so a merge is detected whoever or whatever performed it.
18	
19	This explains more of the machinery than any other single fact about it, which is
20	why it has a page of its own to be pointed at rather than a paragraph repeated in
21	each place it decides something.

1	# What an agent can reach
2	
3	Every run starts with a set of tool servers, and `tools` in `config.yaml` is
4	**additive**: the set is Atomaton's own, and what you write there is added to it.
5	
6	The shipped servers are not in your config. They ship as data, in
7	`.github/atomaton-runtime/tools/defaults.yaml`, in the same schema as
8	`tools.servers`, and that file is there to be **read** — overriding a shipped
9	server means being able to see the entry you are overriding: its `command`, its
10	`args`, what its `env` actually routes. It is not yours to edit, because it is
11	under the runtime root and an upgrade replaces it. `.github/atomaton/README.md`
12	says why they sit there rather than in the file you own.
13	
14	An agent receives the servers its own `mcp_servers` names and no others, so a
15	server nobody names is never started and costs nothing. That is why there is no
16	way to remove one: there is nothing to gain by it, and
17	[naming one that does not exist stops the run](when-it-breaks.md#a-name-that-is-not-a-server)
18	before a single tool starts.
19	
20	## Why these rather than off-the-shelf servers
21	
22	`files` replaces `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem`, which has no line
23	range and no content search. Measured over two runs of these agents, 202 tool
24	calls: 37 of the 63 shell calls were `sed -n A,Bp` and `grep -rn`, rebuilding
25	both by hand. The reviewer, which has no shell, could not — it read one
26	1,700-line file four times with `head` and `tail`, which never reach the middle,
27	and 43% of everything it read came back truncated.
28	
29	That is also the reason `read` reports the offset to continue from: the four
30	reads happened because nothing said that the number being changed did not decide
31	how much came back.
32	
33	## One server, two entries
34	
35	Two of the shipped servers are the same program as another one with tools
36	withheld: `files_readonly` is `files` without the three that write, and
37	`atomaton_env` is `atomaton` with everything but `reload_environment` withheld.
38	
39	The second case is why the pattern exists. `reload_environment` is for whoever is
40	doing the work — the engineer, which is the agent that finds a dependency
41	missing. The other tools on that server are the atomaton's:
42	`request_close_issue` calls itself "the ONLY correct way for the atomaton to
43	finish an issue", and an engineer that could call it could end an issue without a
44	review. So the server cannot simply be handed over.
45	
46	An allowlist is how this project solves that, rather than a second
47	implementation. The cost is a second process of the same script and a longer tool
48	name the agent reads. Both are visible, which is the point — the alternative is
49	one server whose tools mean different things depending on who called them.
50	
51	The same shape is available to you: an entry under `tools.servers` naming a
52	shipped server and a narrower `hooks` block
53	[replaces that server's](reference.md#toolsservers), which is the direction an
54	allowlist has to compose in.
55	
56	`delegate` and `delegate_readonly` are the same pattern applied to a different
57	question. They are one program started with a different definition and a different
58	tools file, and what differs is what the SUB-RUN may reach rather than what the
59	caller may call. The pair exists because a sub-run's servers must be a subset of
60	its caller's: the reviewer holds `files_readonly`, and a delegate that could write
61	would put a writing server one tool call away from an agent whose whole tool set
62	says it cannot change anything. Their definitions live under the runtime root
63	rather than in `agent-definitions/`, because that directory is the namespace a
64	person dispatches from and a delegate is started by a tool. See
65	[delegating a piece of work](how-it-works/delegating-a-piece-of-work.md).

1	# What an agent's pull request meets
2	
3	Opening one starts nothing by itself — [GitHub raises no event for its own
4	token](../work/how-it-works/github-raises-no-event-for-its-own-token.md) — so
5	`create_pr` dispatches `atomaton-validate-pr.yml` as its last act. That workflow
6	runs the configured CI on the branch, writes the result as a check run, and then
7	dispatches whoever the result calls for: the reviewer **named in the call** when it
8	is green, the engineer when it is not.
9	
10	## When nobody is named to look at it
11	
12	Asking explicitly means it can be forgotten. An agent that opens a pull request with
13	no `reviewer` and mentions nobody leaves work that nothing is scheduled to look at —
14	CI runs, the check goes green, and it waits.
15	
16	So the machinery checks and says so, on the pull request:
17	
18	> This pull request was opened by `engineer` with no reviewer named and nobody
19	> mentioned, so nothing is scheduled to look at it. CI still runs and its result
20	> stands. Comment `/reviewer` to have it reviewed, or take it from here.
21	
22	Addressed to whoever the run resolves as the person to notify.
23	
24	## When the check on the deliverable fails
25	
26	Before your CI is asked to run at all, the pull request is checked for whether the
27	`.github/atomaton/` it would merge can still start a run —
28	[what a pull request is checked against](boundaries.md#what-a-pull-request-is-checked-against).
29	
30	When that fails, the required check goes red, the problems are listed in a comment
31	on the pull request, and the engineer is dispatched to fix them — the same handling
32	as failing CI, including the retry limit. The agent sent to fix it is unaffected by
33	the breakage, because a run reads its machinery from
34	[the default branch](../pipeline/how-it-works.md) rather than from the pull request.

1	# Work is a tree of issues
2	
3	An atomaton files sub-issues under the issue it was given; an engineer opens a
4	pull request under the issue it delivers. Each of those is a node, each has at most
5	one parent, and a pull request is a leaf.
6	
7	You act on a node and mean the work under it, so both commands reach the whole
8	subtree:
9	
10	| | reach | ending | undone by |
11	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
12	| `/stop` | the node and everything under it | held | `/resume` over the same subtree |
13	| close | the node and everything under it | over | nothing; reopening is not undo |
14	
15	**They differ in finality, not in reach.** Stop holds the work; close ends it.
16	
17	There used to be an asymmetry here, and it showed up as a checklist: a `/stop` on a
18	parent listed the sub-issues it had not reached and asked you to go and stop each one.
19	That was the machinery turning the narrowness of its own vocabulary into your manual
20	work.
21	
22	**Nothing is stored.** A node is resumable when it is open, nothing is running on it,
23	and its last run ended on a stop — all readable from the tree and the thread. So
24	`/resume` does not replay a record of what a `/stop` covered; it asks the same
25	question again. There is still no paused state to get stuck in.
26	
27	**A merged pull request has left the tree.** GitHub cannot reopen one, so there is
28	nothing there to stop and nothing to close, and a close passes over it.
29	
30	The two commands themselves are
31	[stop a run and pick it up again](../tasks/stop-a-run-and-pick-it-up-again.md) and
32	[close an issue a run is working on](../tasks/close-an-issue-a-run-is-working-on.md).

## What I concluded

This repository is **the delivery template** — the GitHub-side half of an agent delivery system: the workflows, agent definitions, prompt template, skills, MCP tool servers and hooks, and the one policy file that decides what a pull request is checked against, what may merge, which credential reaches which tool server, and how many runs a chain gets. **Atoma core** ([`yuma-seno/atoma`](https://github.com/yuma-seno/atoma)) is the engine it embeds: a stateless Rust CLI that runs the inference loop, speaks MCP to those servers over stdio, and saves the session. The seam between them is one sentence, and everything below is an instance of it: **the template owns every path and every policy; the core owns the loop, and every path it uses arrives as a command-line argument.** Read that way, "is this the template or the engine" stops being guesswork.

What follows is the explanation the issue asked for, then how I know it, what I could not establish, and what happens next.

---

## 1. What it is

Atomaton is, in its own README's words, "a copyable GitHub Actions delivery system powered by [Atoma](https://github.com/yuma-seno/atoma), not Atoma core itself" (`README.md:3-4`). You install it by extracting a release asset — `atomaton-delivery.zip`, which holds `.github/` at its root — into a repository (`README.md:24-38`). After that, a repository member names an agent on an issue or a comment and a GitHub Actions run starts that agent; the agent works in the repository, comments its result back, and dispatches the next agent when one is asked for (`README.md:17-23`).

It is not a hosted product and not a library. It is a tree of files you adopt, exploit and diverge from, and the repository you are reading is both its source and its first adopter: it builds the template under `src/`, and it runs the template under `.github/` (`self/atomaton/skills/project/conventions.md:5-40`).

## 2. The thinking behind it

The ideas are written down, and the repository treats the writing-down as part of the system rather than as commentary.

**Environment-Driven Development.** `docs/method/edd.md` is "the idea the rest of this is an argument for". Its centre is that the environment an agent runs in is itself a development target, improved from what it recorded about its own runs: "The information needed to improve the environment stays inside the environment; the environment is changed on the basis of that information; and the change takes effect on the next run" (`docs/method/edd.md:43-47`). The method's failure list is a list of ways the loop opens — a reason not kept, a fix applied to the run instead of to the environment, a change that does not reach execution.

That is not decoration. The agent prompt template itself tells the agent: "A gap belongs in the environment, not in this run. Working around something broken finishes this run and leaves the next one to meet it again" (`src/content/prompt-template.md:19-25`). And the repository keeps records so the loop can close: the session and the working directory survive on a branch called `atomaton-data` (`docs/records/how-it-works.md:1-19`), and `/tmp/atomaton-workspace` is restored on every run of the same issue (`docs/records/how-it-works.md:21-44`).

**Trust is opt-in on both sides.** An agent only starts because a repository member asked: "An agent only starts when a repository member triggered it" (`docs/work/boundaries.md:5-6`). Opening a pull request, pushing to one or leaving a review starts nobody (`docs/work/how-it-works/what-starts-a-run.md:9-11`). So an outside contributor cannot spend your model budget, and no untrusted text reaches an agent as an instruction.

**Convention over configuration for structure, configuration for policy.** Paths under `.github/` are not settings and deliberately so (`.github/atomaton/README.md:142-169`): a path is how a reader recognises what a file is, and three mechanisms — the ACL that grants the tool user read on the machinery root, the governed-path merge gate, and upgrades that replace directories *by position* — all break at once if you move one. Settings describe policy: what to check, what may merge, what a tool may reach (`.github/atomaton/README.md:182-183`).

**Hide what breaks; show what degrades.** The split between `.github/atomaton/` (yours) and `.github/atomaton-runtime/` (upstream's) is drawn on that line, not on tidiness: deleting a tool server stops a run before the first tool call, while editing a skill or a prompt template merely produces a worse-informed agent (`.github/atomaton/README.md:78-82`). The same line explains why the ten shipped tool servers live in the runtime rather than in `config.yaml`.

## 3. What is technically interesting

- **A pipeline an agent can write.** GitHub refuses `GITHUB_TOKEN` a write under `.github/workflows/**` by identity, on every path and branch, so the template expresses CI and deployment as *commands* in `config.yaml`, under `checks` and `deploy`. As `docs/pipeline/overview.md:36-38` puts it: "An agent can write this file, which is the reason the shape exists at all. GitHub refuses `GITHUB_TOKEN` a write under `.github/workflows/**` by identity, on every path and every branch, and no permission grants it — so a pipeline expressed as YAML there is a pipeline an agent can read and never maintain." The generated workflows are fixed shells that run whatever the config names.
- **Two roots, one rule.** "Two roots, and the line between them is **declaration versus mechanism** — stated first in `deploy-jobs.ts`: *an agent can write configuration and cannot write a workflow*" (`docs/template/architecture.md:124-128`). `src/content/` deploys to `.github/atomaton/`; `src/entrypoints/machinery/` deploys to `.github/atomaton-runtime/scripts/`; `src/entrypoints/tools/` to `.github/atomaton-runtime/tools/`. A `BUILT_FROM` table in `src/domain/machinery/machinery-layout.ts:237-241` records that correspondence as data, because the source names and the deployed names no longer resemble each other.
- **The tools file is generated per run and thrown away.** `tools.servers` in `config.yaml` is the core's own tools-file format, one level in; `src/entrypoints/machinery/write_tools_file.ts` writes the real file into `$RUNNER_TEMP/atomaton-run/` for that run only (`src/domain/machinery/machinery-layout.ts:97-113`). Shipping it previously gave a repository a config and a generated file that nothing could regenerate from the other.
- **Tool servers run as one dedicated OS user with no sudo.** The reasoning is unusually concrete: `PR_SET_DUMPABLE(0)` does not survive `execve` (`docs/tools/boundaries.md:168-172`), `LD_PRELOAD` would have closed both holes but fails on `gh`, "which is written in Go and statically linked: a static binary ignores `LD_PRELOAD` entirely" (`docs/tools/boundaries.md:174-179`), and a different uid closes the environment hole outright (`docs/tools/boundaries.md:181-183`). The result is a documented trade rather than a claim of isolation: three properties cannot all hold, and the one given up — arbitrary third-party servers cannot be protected — is stated plainly.
- **Credentials are routed, not inherited.** A tool server receives only what its own `env:` names, and anything the core recognises as a credential is removed from its environment first, so `env: {}` means "no credentials" (`docs/tools/how-it-works/routing-a-credential.md:1-25`). `tools.secrets` says what a run may hold; a server's `env` says which server sees it. Authorising is not delivering.
- **Two caps on the same text, on purpose and with the relationship written down.** This repository's servers cap themselves at `TOOL_OUTPUT_BUDGET = 50_000` characters (`src/shared/tool-output.ts:50`) and pass `max_output_chars = TOOL_OUTPUT_BACKSTOP` (100,000) to the core for servers this repository wrote (`src/domain/machinery/tools-file.ts:92-93`), because the core caps every result on the client and JSON escaping can add a second character for every one of the first 50,000. Then a *third* cap shortens each result to 4,000 characters on the way into a session (`src/domain/work/session-size.ts:81`), with the measurement that chose the number in the same file.
- **The contract tests.** `tests/contract/` holds 29 files, each written to make a specific silent drift loud: `layering.test.ts` fails on an import arrow that points outward; `doc-links.test.ts` resolves every relative link and anchor between documents; `self-overlay.test.ts` requires `self/X` and `.github/X` byte-identical in both directions; `test-script.test.ts` asserts that every path the `test` script names exists, because "`bun test <path that does not exist>` does not fail" (`tests/contract/test-script.test.ts:9-12`). These are the files that turn red when documentation and implementation drift apart, and they are the fastest way to see what is genuinely fixed here.
- **Bounds that are counts of runs, not of tokens.** `chain.after_handoffs: 5` and `chain.after_runs_without_change: 2` stop a chain, and `environment.max_reloads: 3` bounds environment rebuilds; nothing bounds cost (`docs/work/boundaries.md:36-47`, `docs/work/reference.md:43-74`). The reasoning for two counters rather than one is a measured argument that a count of runs is a poor proxy in both directions (`docs/work/how-it-works/why-there-are-two-counters.md:12-18`).
- **Post-merge work is dispatched, never listened for**, because GitHub starts no workflow run for an event its own token triggered (`docs/work/how-it-works/github-raises-no-event-for-its-own-token.md:1-17`). That single fact explains most of the explicit `workflow_dispatch` calls in the tree.

## 4. What to read first to start using it

1. `README.md` — what it is and the five-minute install (extract the release asset at your repository root).
2. `docs/setup.md` — the ordered path from an empty repository to a first run. Seven steps, and three of them are things nothing will tell you if you skip: enable Actions, allow Actions to create pull requests, and apply the branch ruleset. The one credential the shipped configuration needs is `ORCAROUTER_API_KEY` (`docs/setup.md:16-23`).
3. `docs/README.md` — the map. It is indexed by what you want to change and by what went wrong, so it is how you find the page for a symptom instead of reading everything.
4. `.github/atomaton/README.md` — the walk through the directory you own, and the table of the ten tool servers, three agents and three+one skills that ship.
5. `docs/config/reference.md` — every key `config.yaml` accepts, with a link to the entry that explains it.

## 5. What to read first to contribute to it

1. `CONTRIBUTING.md` — above all its "source-of-truth map": `src/` is the deliverable, `dist/.github/` is generated and untracked, `scripts/` is this repository's own pipeline, `self/` is this repository's four-or-so own files overlaid onto `.github/`, and `tests/` tests the machinery rather than the shipped behaviour.
2. `docs/template/architecture.md` — the layering rule (arrows point inward; `domain` is pure; `adapters` touches the outside; `entrypoints` are thin), the four domain contexts, where the deployed tree splits, and an explicit list of open questions. It is the one page whose subject is the template's own source, and `docs/README.md` says so.
3. `tests/contract/` — read the module comment at the top of each file. Every one of them names the defect it exists to prevent, and that is the most compact statement of this project's conventions that exists.
4. The commands: `bun install`, then `bun run typecheck`, `bun run synth`, `bun run test`, `bun run test:e2e` (`CONTRIBUTING.md:225-243`). `test:e2e` runs against the built tree, so `synth` has to come first.
5. The rule that catches most newcomers: `.github/` is **deployed, not generated on merge** — it is a release plus `self/` copied over it (`CONTRIBUTING.md:275-283`). A change under `src/` reaches the live agents here only after a self-deploy is dispatched, and a change to `self/X` must be made identically in `.github/X` in the same pull request.

## Atoma core, and where the line falls

**What it is.** Atoma core is a Rust CLI in a separate repository, `yuma-seno/atoma`, described there as "a stateless MCP orchestrator CLI for running agent definitions against LLM providers and tool servers". It parses an agent definition, builds a system prompt, calls an OpenAI-compatible provider, executes MCP tool calls in a loop, and writes a session file. Here it is installed on the runner as a release asset at `/usr/local/bin/atoma` (`src/workflows/actions/atoma-cli.ts:216-238`), or, when the dispatch asks for `atoma_version: source`, checked out and built with `cargo install --path atoma-src --force --locked` from `main` (`src/workflows/actions/atoma-cli.ts:202-206`, and the `source` branch of the installer). The version a run installs unless told otherwise is one constant, `ATOMA_DEFAULT_VERSION` in `src/workflows/actions/atoma-cli.ts:190`, used by three workflows from one place.

**What it owns.** The inference loop and turn boundaries; the provider dialect and credential resolution; the session file's content and semantics; MCP transports (stdio, and Streamable HTTP from v0.1.19); the repetition circuit breaker behind `--loop-retries`; the client-side cap on every tool result; and the meaning of each flag — `--stop-file` checked at the top of a turn, `--max-runtime-secs`, and so on. Its own `run --help` is the authority for that list; the invocation the runner builds is visible in full at `src/workflows/atomaton-runner.wac.ts:873-885`:

  atoma run \

> The core has no project of its own — it is handed a layout and works in whatever it is given. **This deliverable is the layout.** The core's configurability is the seam Atomaton passes these paths through, which is why they are settled here and not again in your config.

That is also why `src/workflows/actions/atoma-cli.ts` carries a long, version-by-version comment: every raise of the pin has been coupled to a declaration made on this side — `${NAME}` expansion in a server's `env` and `args` (v0.1.11, v0.1.12), the provider table and per-provider credentials (v0.1.13), `agent-definitions/*.md` (v0.1.14), `request_timeout_secs` per server and JSON-RPC id matching (v0.1.17), attaching a degraded-server report to the next tool result (v0.1.18), `--max-runtime-secs` (v0.1.22), `--stop-file` (v0.1.23), saving a session whatever ended the run (v0.1.24), loop guards (v0.1.25), cache accounting (v0.1.43), per-definition request headers (v0.1.44), `load_skill`'s single argument spelling (v0.1.45), and `--loop-retries` (v0.1.46). **Where the four named behaviours fall.** This is the part a reader who knows only one project cannot infer:

| Behaviour | Which side | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The merge gate** | Template | `merge.policy`, `merge.governed_paths` and `merge.gates` in `config.yaml`, plus the branch ruleset in `.github/atomaton/rulesets/main.json`; enforced by the `github__*` MCP server through `src/domain/delivery/merge-readiness.ts` and `src/adapters/github/merge-signals.ts`. **Why they are separate.** The core has no project, no repository layout, no GitHub vocabulary and no opinion about what a merge is. The template has all of those and no inference loop. Each can change without the other only because the coupling between them is an explicit argv list and a pinned version with its couplings written down — which is exactly what makes "which project does this behaviour belong to" answerable from the repository rather than from memory.
